hypotheses.title: Rate-limit windows grow without eviction; pinned deletes each key on a per-key timeout
hypotheses.reproducerPlan: in-package test: limiter.consume(key_i, t0) for 10000 distinct keys, advance past the window, then read len(entries) (test may live in package server); pinned's equivalent drops each key by timer. Today the map retains every key forever. Measure RSS in the M5 soak with a concurrent distinct-source load.
hypotheses.counterargument: keys are client IPs, so a flood needs many real sources unless rateLimiting.preferRealIpHeader is on (then the key embeds an attacker-controlled header, accounts.go:1531-1543); successful logins clear their own key. The 429 shape is unaffected, so this is a memory/stability risk rather than a wrong response.

hypotheses.title: Settings saves are process-wide serialized across disk I/O, but pinned serializes more (single event loop), so this is parity-or-better
hypotheses.reproducerPlan: recorded as the R2 counterargument: before proposing a per-user coordinator, measure Go p50/p95/p99 against pinned Node on the same host and load (C-H3) and show any user-visible timeout; the save->backup ordering, duplicate-aware snapshot and 10-minute trailing edge must be preserved by any redesign.
hypotheses.counterargument: a per-user design would be LESS serialized than the oracle; the plan's R2 says only if red tests justify it, and no red test exists yet. The one cost not present in pinned is the cross-process flock (C-H4).

hypotheses.title: Cross-user settings-save latency under contention is unmeasured; no test drives two handles concurrently
hypotheses.reproducerPlan: E06 leg: 8 synthetic users, one 5 MB settings body each, 200 concurrent saves per user against a real handler; record p50/p95/p99 per user and max queue depth; run the same load on pinned Node for the comparison C-H2 predicts. Pass: Go p99 <= pinned p99 and no request exceeds pinned's own save block.
hypotheses.counterargument: the mechanism is source-proven; only the magnitude is unknown, and C-H2 predicts parity-or-better. If measured latency is worse than pinned's, that is the red test R2 needs.

hypotheses.title: settingsSaveMu is held while acquiring a data-root-wide flock bounded at 10s, so a second process stalls every user's save
hypotheses.reproducerPlan: two-process test (the pattern of alpha.15 B-07): process A holds the data-root flock (or sleeps inside the lock), process B posts settings/save for 3 users and measures per-user latency; assert the wait stays within the recorded budget and that a second process does not turn a 200 into an unbounded wait.
hypotheses.counterargument: pinned has no cross-process lock and silently tears settings (audit B-07); the lock is a deliberate data-safety addition. A redesign that releases L1 before the snapshot could shorten the queue without weakening the write lock, but must keep the duplicate check ordered after the write.

hypotheses.title: The trailing settings-backup timer is detached and never stopped/awaited on shutdown; a pending snapshot is lost, as in pinned
hypotheses.reproducerPlan: if a later release decides to flush pending snapshots, the test is: save twice (second sets pending), stop the server, assert a backup exists. Today the test must STOP the timer manually (settings_save_test.go:231), which is the evidence that no shutdown path flushes it.
hypotheses.counterargument: settings.json is already persisted by the request; the snapshot is a duplicate-aware convenience. pinned's SIGINT path is process.exit() without flushing the throttle timer, so flushing would be a NEW guarantee, not parity.

hypotheses.title: Graceful shutdown has an unbounded wait: heartbeat.stop waits on the writer mutex and done channel outside the ctx
hypotheses.reproducerPlan: add a heartbeat write seam (the project's existing test-seam pattern, e.g. internal/app/server.go:409-418) that a test can block; call RunningServer.Close with a 100ms ctx while the write is held; assert Close returns within a stated bound with a named error. Today it hangs.
hypotheses.counterargument: a local fsync rarely stalls, and the write is small; but AGENTS rule 24/Rule 33 say a wait without a named bound is the shape a user-visible hang takes, and this is the shutdown path a user triggers with Ctrl+C.

hypotheses.title: Second Ctrl+C promises 'in-flight requests are aborted' but only closes listeners; the deferred Close can still wait 10s
hypotheses.reproducerPlan: in-process test: handler blocks until released; start the server, deliver signal 1 then signal 2 through shutdownAfterSignal and measure the time until Close returns. Assert it is within a short bound and that the message matches behaviour (either close active connections or change the text).
hypotheses.counterargument: pinned's SIGINT is an immediate process.exit with no drain, so Go's 10s drain is already more graceful; the defect is the message/behaviour mismatch, not the drain itself. The process does exit 130.

hypotheses.title: The -race gate omits internal/app and internal/lockacquire; the real signal path has no test
hypotheses.reproducerPlan: add ./internal/app ./internal/lockacquire to the race job's package list (cheap) and add the concurrent-Close/second-signal test from C-H7; run it in CI (this host cannot run -race: windows/arm64).
hypotheses.counterargument: http.Server.Shutdown, listener.Close and the heartbeat's sync.Once are idempotent by construction, so the concurrent Close is probably safe; but the gate's own comment says it covers the packages that own shared state, and internal/app owns a mutex+Once+goroutine. Rule 104 makes the detector the only oracle here.

hypotheses.title: Comfy/RunPod poll loops have no attempt bound and keep the handler goroutine after the client leaves (pinned parity)
hypotheses.reproducerPlan: M5 soak: pin one Comfy job that never completes, disconnect the client, and observe goroutine/RSS growth. Compare with pinned's promise chain on the same scenario; only a divergence would be a finding.
hypotheses.counterargument: pinned has while(true) too; the Go side actually frees the connection when the client leaves but keeps the handler. A bound would be a deliberate divergence, so it needs a product decision (like the docker-DNS bound).

hypotheses.title: Two unbounded process-wide sets are reproduced from pinned (cache-buster keys, access-log IPs); the host-whitelist cap is parity too
hypotheses.reproducerPlan: no reproducer needed for parity; if a later release hardens them, that is a visible product decision and needs a memory-bound + a test that the 304/header behaviour is unchanged.
hypotheses.counterargument: hard rule 5 says inherited weaknesses are reproduced and recorded rather than silently fixed; both sets are client-controlled, so growth is possible in both products equally.

hypotheses.title: The same-size+same-mtime residual is closed for the account cache with ctime on Unix but open in the two response caches although they already stat every input
hypotheses.reproducerPlan: extend the existing residual tests: externally replace a preset/card with same-size content and os.Chtimes back to the original mtime, then GET through the route. On Unix the account cache already returns the new value (change stamp), while the response caches serve the old body. Decide: add the change stamp (no extra syscall) or record the difference as accepted.
hypotheses.counterargument: no product writer can produce it (atomicReplace moves mtime and, on Unix, ctime), and Windows has no stat-available change stamp so the boundary would remain there. The residual is already documented and pinned by tests, so this is a recorded decision unless the user-visible stale read is judged unacceptable.

hypotheses.title: internal/outbound wire-exact path starts one goroutine per connection released only by ctx/socket close; it is a probe client, not the production transport
hypotheses.reproducerPlan: no action in M0; if wire-exact mode is ever used for a long-running soak, pass a cancellable context and assert the goroutine count returns to baseline (server_soak_test.go is the template).
hypotheses.counterargument: the path is reachable only with GOTAVERN_OUTBOUND_WIRE_EXACT=1 and AGENTS rule 30 forbids it carrying user traffic; production uses the net/http client with bounded timeouts.

questions: Can this lane's claims about the shutdown path be measured at all without a seam? H6/H7 need either a blocking-FS seam or a new test hook; M0 may not add one, so the reproducers are named but unrun. Lane E / the Lead should decide whether the shared seam belongs in alpha.16.

Do we have a pinned oracle for the graceful-shutdown drain time? Pinned exits immediately on SIGINT (src/server-main.js:318-331), so Go's 10s drain has no pinned counterpart; H7's message should be judged as a GoTavern UX statement, not a parity claim.

Should the rate-limit sweep (H1) be fixed in alpha.16 R5? It is the only found unbounded production map that is NOT pinned parity, and the fix is local (a sweep or a bounded map). It needs the Lead's priority call and a failing test per M0 rule 2.

Tokenizer set caches (C7 / L11) have no measured benefit, which is a GOAL 15.3 gap. Is a before/after bench required before any change, or is 'vendored assets, no disk-cache switch' an acceptable recorded justification?

The race job's package list (H8) is a decision for whoever owns .github/workflows/ci.yml; adding internal/app + internal/lockacquire is cheap but changes the gate, so it must be its own commit with a demonstrated red on a planted race.

source-graph facts[] undercount primitives inside package-level var initializers and var type expressions (report 7.2). Does the Lead want the generator taught about those, or is globals[] + per-lane grep the accepted method for M0 coverage?
